hook: Buying a house in Massachusetts can get expensive before you even get the keys.
tags: how to buy a house in Massachusetts
how much house can I afford in Massachusetts
title: How to Buy a House in Massachusetts Without Costly Surprises

scenes.text: That listing price is only the beginning. The real decision is whether you can afford the house, its location, and everything ownership brings. Massachusetts isn't one housing market. Prices, property types, and competition change dramatically between communities, and sometimes between neighborhoods within the same town.
scenes.subject: house exterior

scenes.text: So before you start chasing listings, build a buying plan. We'll follow the process from your first budget to getting the keys. Start with a monthly payment you can actually live with, not the biggest mortgage a lender is willing to approve for you.

visual.sub: Approval is not the same as comfort
visual.headline: BUDGET BEFORE HOUSE HUNTING

scenes.subject: homebuyers planning

scenes.text: Your housing budget should include mortgage principal and interest, property taxes, homeowners insurance, and any mortgage insurance or association dues that apply. Then add the costs outside that payment: heating, electricity, water, maintenance, and transportation. A manageable mortgage can still hide an uncomfortable monthly budget. Keep an emergency reserve separate from your down payment. If buying empties your savings, even an ordinary repair can become a financial crisis.
scenes.subject: mortgage paperwork

scenes.text: Your upfront cash has several jobs: the down payment, closing costs, prepaid expenses, and reserves. Don't treat those as one interchangeable pot. Closing costs can include lender charges, appraisal fees, title services, recording fees, and legal expenses. Your actual amount depends on the transaction.
scenes.subject: homebuyer documents

scenes.text: Before applying, review your credit reports and existing debts. Correct errors early, and avoid taking on new borrowing while preparing to buy. Gather pay records, bank statements, tax documents, and information about your debts. Self-employed buyers may need additional documentation to establish qualifying income. Next, get preapproved. Preapproval is more useful than a casual affordability estimate, but it is not a guarantee that your loan will close.

visual.sub: Preapproved means guaranteed
visual.headline: FINAL APPROVAL STILL HAS CONDITIONS

scenes.subject: credit review

scenes.text: The property must qualify too, and your finances will be checked again. A job change or new car payment can complicate underwriting. Compare more than the advertised interest rate. Request Loan Estimates and examine fees, points, mortgage insurance, and the cash required at closing.

visual.headline: THE PROPERTY MUST QUALIFY TOO, AND YOUR

scenes.subject: mortgage applicant

scenes.text: For a meaningful comparison, ask lenders about the same loan type and similar rate-lock terms. Otherwise, the cheapest-looking offer may not be cheapest. Check legitimate assistance before assuming you cannot buy. MassHousing and the Massachusetts Housing Partnership's ONE Mortgage are programs worth researching through official sources. Eligibility and available assistance can change. Income limits, purchase-price limits, education requirements, and participating lenders may determine whether a particular program fits you.

visual.sub: MassHousing and ONE Mortgage
visual.headline: CHECK ASSISTANCE EARLY

scenes.subject: lender consultation

scenes.text: A homebuyer education course can help you understand financing and ownership obligations. Some assistance programs require an approved course before you can qualify. Now narrow your search around daily life. Think about your workplace, caregiving responsibilities, transportation options, and how long you expect to stay.

visual.headline: A HOMEBUYER EDUCATION COURSE CAN HELP YOU

scenes.subject: homebuyer class

scenes.text: A lower purchase price farther away can mean higher transportation costs and less time at home. Compare the entire routine, not just bedrooms. Test the commute when you would actually make it. A relaxed weekend drive tells you very little about a typical weekday morning. Visit your target neighborhood at different times. Look for street lighting, parking pressure, nearby activity, and noise that listing photographs cannot reveal.
scenes.subject: commuter driving

scenes.text: Research property taxes directly with the municipality. The seller's current bill may reflect exemptions or circumstances that won't carry over to you. Choose representation deliberately. Ask a buyer's agent about local experience, communication, services, and compensation, and read any representation agreement before signing it.

visual.sub: Read the agreement before signing
visual.headline: UNDERSTAND WHO REPRESENTS YOU

scenes.subject: town hall

scenes.text: Ask a Massachusetts real estate attorney to explain the contract process early. Discovering an important obligation after signing can leave you fewer options. When touring houses, separate cosmetic preferences from expensive systems. An outdated paint color is very different from a failing roof or recurring water intrusion. Look closely at the basement. Staining, musty odors, fresh patches, and stored items raised off the floor can justify questions about water history.
scenes.subject: real estate attorney

scenes.text: Ask about the roof, heating system, electrical service, and drainage. Their age and condition can matter more than the kitchen's appearance during ownership. Massachusetts has many older homes. Age alone isn't a dealbreaker, but older construction can bring maintenance needs that deserve specialist evaluation before purchase.
scenes.subject: home inspector

scenes.text: Ask what heats the home, and request available fuel-use records. Oil, gas, electric resistance, and heat pumps can produce very different operating costs. For homes built before 1978, lead-paint disclosures deserve attention. Massachusetts also has lead-law obligations involving homes where children under six live. An inspection can identify concerns, but it cannot promise a problem-free house. Ask about its scope, exclusions, and whether additional specialist inspections make sense.

visual.sub: An inspection guarantees the house
visual.headline: INSPECTIONS HAVE LIMITS

scenes.subject: heating technician

scenes.text: Radon testing is worth discussing because you cannot judge radon levels by appearance or smell. Follow current public-health guidance when interpreting the results. If the property uses a private well, investigate water quality and supply. A clean-looking glass of water cannot establish that a well is safe.

visual.headline: RADON TESTING IS WORTH DISCUSSING BECAUSE YOU

scenes.subject: radon testing

scenes.text: For a home with a septic system, understand Massachusetts Title 5 inspection requirements, applicable exceptions, and who would handle any required corrective work. Check flood exposure before committing, even away from the coast. Standard homeowners insurance generally excludes flood damage, and separate coverage may be necessary. Get an insurance quote while you still have time to investigate. Roof condition, claims history, and location can affect availability and cost.

visual.sub: Standard coverage generally excludes flood damage
visual.headline: CHECK FLOOD RISK EARLY

scenes.subject: septic inspection

scenes.text: Buying a condominium adds another layer. You are purchasing your unit and joining an association whose finances and decisions can affect your budget. Review the condominium documents, budget, reserves, meeting records, insurance, and pending litigation with qualified help. Ask directly about upcoming projects and special assessments.
scenes.subject: condominium entrance

scenes.text: A low condo fee isn't automatically a bargain. Inadequate reserves can leave major building work funded through additional charges to individual owners. Also check rules affecting your plans, including pets, rentals, parking, and renovations. Confirm that your lender can finance the particular condominium project. Considering a multifamily property? Potential rental income comes with landlord responsibilities, maintenance obligations, and legal rules. Don't budget as though every month is guaranteed.

visual.sub: Lower condo fees always mean savings
visual.headline: LOW FEES CAN HIDE COSTS

scenes.subject: condo roof repairs

scenes.text: For any property, investigate permits for significant alterations. A finished attic or basement in a listing isn't proof of approved living space. When a house fits, evaluate comparable recent sales before choosing an offer price. The asking price is a marketing decision, not independent proof of value.

visual.sub: The asking price is only a starting point
visual.headline: PRICE AGAINST RECENT SALES

scenes.subject: finished attic

scenes.text: Set your walk-away number before negotiations become emotional. Include repairs and likely ownership costs, rather than stretching simply because another offer might exist. An offer involves more than price: deposit, financing, inspection terms, timing, and other conditions can all change your financial exposure if something goes wrong. Massachusetts offers can create binding obligations. Have your attorney explain the language and deadlines rather than assuming nothing counts until the later contract.

visual.headline: SET YOUR WALK-AWAY NUMBER BEFORE NEGOTIATIONS BECOME

scenes.subject: couple discussing

scenes.text: Massachusetts now protects buyers' home inspection rights in covered transactions. Have your attorney explain current requirements, exceptions, and how your inspection terms work. A financing contingency can offer protection if your loan falls through, but wording and deadlines matter. It is not an unlimited escape clause.

visual.sub: Confirm current rules and contract terms
visual.headline: KNOW YOUR INSPECTION RIGHTS

scenes.subject: inspection consultation

scenes.text: Keep deposits and deadlines organized. Whether a deposit is refundable depends on the agreement and circumstances, so never rely on a verbal reassurance. After acceptance, the purchase and sale agreement typically sets out more detailed terms. Review included fixtures, promised work, contingencies, and the closing date. Your lender's appraisal is different from your inspection. The appraisal addresses value for lending purposes; the inspection examines the property's condition within its scope.
scenes.subject: buyer calendar

scenes.text: If the appraisal comes in below the purchase price, your financing may change. Your options depend on available cash, negotiation, and contract protections. During underwriting, respond promptly to document requests. Avoid moving large sums without documentation, opening new credit, or making major purchases without consulting your lender.

visual.headline: IF THE APPRAISAL COMES IN BELOW THE

scenes.subject: appraisal discussion

scenes.text: Ask your closing attorney about title review, ownership, and title insurance. Understand the distinction between coverage protecting the lender and coverage protecting you. Treat wire instructions as a fraud risk. Verify them by calling a trusted, independently confirmed number, especially if payment instructions suddenly change. For most purchase mortgages, you must receive the initial Closing Disclosure at least three business days before closing. Use that time to review carefully.

visual.headline: ASK YOUR CLOSING ATTORNEY ABOUT TITLE REVIEW,

scenes.subject: closing attorney

scenes.text: Compare that disclosure with your Loan Estimate. Question unexpected fees, confirm your loan terms, and verify the final amount you need to bring. Confirm required smoke and carbon monoxide compliance documentation is handled for the sale. Ask your attorney who is responsible and what applies.

visual.headline: COMPARE THAT DISCLOSURE WITH YOUR LOAN ESTIMATE

scenes.subject: document comparison

scenes.text: At the final walkthrough, check agreed repairs, included appliances, and property condition. Confirm the home is being delivered as your contract requires. If something is wrong, raise it before closing. Your attorney can explain possible solutions; an informal promise may not provide meaningful protection. Arrange insurance and utilities for the appropriate dates. Confirm when you legally take possession before booking movers or assuming you can enter.
scenes.subject: final walkthrough

scenes.text: After closing, protect the purchase with a maintenance plan. Clean gutters, service heating equipment, address leaks early, and keep records of major work. Your first year is also a budgeting reality check. Track actual utilities, maintenance, taxes, and insurance, then adjust your reserve contributions accordingly.

visual.sub: Update your budget with actual costs
visual.headline: OWNERSHIP NEEDS A BUFFER

scenes.subject: gutter cleaning

scenes.text: If the numbers don't work yet, waiting can be a sound decision. More savings or a different property type may improve your position. The goal isn't simply to win a house in Massachusetts. It's to buy a home you can keep without sacrificing your financial breathing room. What monthly housing payment would feel comfortable for you in Massachusetts? Share your number in the comments, and like the video if this helped.

visual.headline: IF THE NUMBERS DON'T WORK YET, WAITING
